*Facts:* Several relatives challenged a holographic will appointing a sole heir, alleging the testator’s natural incapacity at the time of execution and, for some claimants, seeking annulment despite the existence of closer intestate heirs.
*Legal framework:* Articles 591(1)(3) and 602 Italian Civil Code; rules on standing and interest to sue; principles on burden of proof in actions for annulment of wills; evidentiary value of court-appointed expert opinions.
*Interpretative issues:* (i) Whether heirs excluded from intestate succession by the presence of lower-degree heirs have standing and interest to challenge a will for natural incapacity; (ii) the legal notion of “natural incapacity” relevant for testamentary annulment and its distinction from mere mental weakness; (iii) allocation of the burden of proof and assessment of medical and circumstantial evidence, including expert findings, to establish incapacity at the precise time of the will.
*Principles applied:* An action for annulment of a will due to natural incapacity is inadmissible for lack of interest when brought by heirs who would not benefit from intestate succession because of the existence of closer heirs; natural incapacity under Article 591 Civil Code requires proof that, at the moment of execution, the testator was entirely incapable of understanding and self-determination, not merely affected by mental disorders; the burden of proving such incapacity lies with the challenger, except in cases of permanent and habitual infirmity, and may be rebutted by evidence of lucidity, coherent content of the will, absence of contemporaneous medical certification, and a reasoned court-appointed expert opinion.
